The Best Pens for Note-Taking
August 13, 2024 - Posted by Connie to Guides, Fountain Pens, Gel Pens, Multi Pens, Pens, Ballpoint Pens, Rollerball Pens, Highlighters

Did you know that taking notes by hand helps you understand a subject better1? Keep reading or watch the video below to learn about the best pens for long note-taking sessions.

THE BEST PEN FOR NOTE-TAKING
Uni Jetstream Alpha Gel Grip Ballpoint Pen
The Uni Jetstream Alpha Gel Grip Ballpoint Pen is the best pen for note-taking thanks to its low-viscosity ink and comfortable grip section.

Shop Now

The best pen for note-taking is the Uni Jetstream Alpha Gel Grip Ballpoint Pen. It has all the features a writer would appreciate in a pen: the low-viscosity, vibrant ink is specially formulated to flow smoothly. It dries almost instantly and doesn’t smear under highlighters. The pen only comes in one 0.7 mm tip size (you can swap out the refill for a different tip size), but we’ve found that it works well for small and large handwriting.

We recommend the Alpha Gel Grip version because it’s well balanced with a squishy silicone grip that’s comfortable to hold, even if you grasp your pen tightly. However, other Jetstream pens—including versions with Lite Touch Ink that require almost no pressure to write—are available, and you can learn about the whole lineup in our guide.

THE BEST PENS FOR NOTE-TAKING RECOMMENDATIONS
The Best Ballpoint Pens for Note-Taking: Pilot Acroball Ballpoint Pens
The Pilot Acroball Ballpoint Pen uses low-viscosity ballpoint ink that won’t smear under highlighters.

Shop Now

While the Uni Jetstream Ballpoint Pen is our top choice for note-taking, the Pilot Acroball is a similar pick that works just as well. It uses low-viscosity ballpoint ink that dries quickly and doesn’t smear under highlighters.

The Acroball Ballpoint Pens have rubber grips so they don’t slip out of your hands. Other pens that use the same ink, such as the Acro 1000 and Acro ILMILY, are a little more expensive and have sleek, modern looks.

Also Consider: Pentel Calme Ballpoint Pens

The Pentel Calme is a minimalist ballpoint pen designed to reduce distraction. Its quiet click mechanism won’t distract those around you, and the textured grip section covers a large portion of the barrel so you don’t have to think about where you’re grasping the pen. Its low-viscosity Vicuña ink flows smoothly, too.

The Best Gel Pens for Note-Taking: Zebra Sarasa Dry Gel Pens
The Zebra Sarasa Dry Gel Pen uses ink that dries almost instantly.

Shop Now

The Zebra Sarasa Dry isn’t just our favorite gel pen for note-taking, it’s one of our favorite gel pens—period. Its ink flows smoothly yet dries almost instantly no matter what paper you use. Even its broadest tip sizes only take a second or two to become completely dry.

It does have a few flaws, however: first, its 0.4 mm, 0.5 mm, and 0.7 mm tip sizes are only available in basic black, red, and blue (the Sarasa Dry X20 comes in more colors but in 0.7 mm and 1.0 mm tip sizes). Second, it smudges under most highlighters. If you must pair your gel pen with highlighters, try the Sarasa Mark On and its specially formulated ink instead.

Learn more about the Zebra Sarasa lineup in our comprehensive guide.

Also Consider: Uni-ball One Gel Pens

The Uni-ball One Gel Pen is a stylish alternative to the Zebra Sarasa Dry. Its innovative ink is made up of large pigment particles that sit on top of the page, so your writing looks more vivid. Color-coders are sure to appreciate the One and its variety of colors, including limited edition options. However, it does smear under highlighters slightly.

As a bonus, a study at Ritsumeikan University in Japan found that students who wrote with a black One could remember information better than students who used ordinary black ink! While the One can’t make up for a good study session, it certainly wouldn’t hurt to use it while you’re taking notes.

The Best Rollerball Pens for Note-Taking: Pilot Precise Rollerball Pens
The Pilot Precise Rollerball Pen has a needlepoint tip that doesn’t feel scratchy.

Shop Now

The Pilot Precise is a great note-taking pen that you might already be familiar with. Its needlepoint tip doesn’t feel scratchy and practically glides across the paper, so very little pressure is needed to make the ink flow.

Like most rollerball pens, the Precise uses a fluid, water-based ink that takes a few seconds to dry. Additionally, it smears easily when highlighted. Thankfully, it comes in plenty of colors, so you can still organize your notes with ease.

Also Consider: Uni-ball Air Rollerball Pens

The Uni-ball Air is one of the smoothest rollerball pens we’ve ever tried. Its tip is surrounded by plastic instead of metal, so it creates less friction when it rubs against the paper.

However, it has a few downsides that prevent us from recommending it more highly. First, it only comes in blue or black ink. Additionally, the 0.5 mm tip size is only available in a pack of three. If you’d just like to give the Air a try instead of committing to a whole pack of pens, you’ll have to get the 0.7 mm tip size.

The Best Multi Pens for Note-Taking: Uni Jetstream 4 Color Ballpoint Multi Pens
The Uni Jetstream 4 Color Ballpoint Multi Pen is a multicolor pen that puts four ballpoint ink colors at your fingertips.

Shop Now

The Uni Jetstream 4 Color is a multicolor pen that puts four ballpoint ink colors at your fingertips, which is especially useful for color-coding notes. It uses the same low-viscosity Jetstream ink that we recommended as our top pick, so it flows smoothly, dries quickly, and doesn’t smear under highlighters.

The multi pen is also available in a 4&1 version that includes a mechanical pencil component. If you don’t need quite as many colors and would prefer more tip sizes, try three-component Jetstream Multi Pens instead.

Also Consider: Uni Style Fit Multi Pens

The Uni Style Fit is a customizable multi pen that lets you pack as many as five different refills into one body. Choose your preferred body, then add your favorite gel, ballpoint, or mechanical pencil components. The gel refills use the same inks found in Signo Gel Pens, while the ballpoint refills use Jetstream inks.

Multi pen refills are smaller than “single” pen refills, and run out of ink faster. Additionally, gel inks are more fluid than ballpoint inks, and will get used up quickly. We recommend using ballpoint ink for the bulk of your notes and color-code with gel inks so you’re not constantly swapping out refills.

You don’t have to use Uni’s refills, though. The multi pen bodies are compatible with refills from different brands. Read our guide to learn more about the Style Fit.

The Best Highlighters for Note-Taking: Zebra Justfit Mojini Line Highlighters
The Zebra Justfit Mojini Line Highlighter uses ink that resists smearing water-based inks.

Shop Now

Zebra Justfit Mojini Line Highlighters are perfect for note-taking because they’re specially formulated to resist smearing water-based inks. In our tests, we found that the Justfit Mojini Line barely smeared gel, rollerball, and fountain pen inks.

The highlighter also has a flexible chisel tip that stays firmly pressed against the page, which makes it easy to highlight over the curved part of a textbook or notebook. It comes in five bright colors that grab your attention.

Also Consider: Kokuyo Mark+ 2 Way Marker Pens

The Kokuyo Mark+ 2 Way Marker Pen is a handy tool for color-coders. It features a highlighter on one end and a fineliner with a complementary color on the other. That way, your notes will always look coordinated! The Kokuyo Mark+ 2 Way will smear water-based inks a bit, but we felt that its color combinations make up for the smudging.

The Best Fountain Pens for Note-Taking: Platinum Preppy Fountain Pens
The high-quality Platinum Preppy Fountain Pen has a budget-friendly price.

Shop Now

Platinum Preppy Fountain Pens are high-quality note-taking tools at budget prices. A fountain pen only works as well as its nib, and the JetPens team is happy to say that the Preppy’s is very smooth. The extra fine nib has a tiny amount of feedback, but we think it’s acceptable for such a precise line.

Each Preppy includes one proprietary cartridge that matches the pen’s barrel (except for the clear pen, which includes a black cartridge). The ink inside dries quickly and works well on regular paper, too—fountain pen friendly paper isn’t a necessity, though we always recommend it. You can also pick up a converter to fill the pen from an ink bottle.

Also Consider: TWSBI GO Fountain Pens

Unlike other entry-level fountain pens, the TWSBI GO doesn’t use cartridges and must be filled from an ink bottle. It’s a great option for beginner fountain pen users who are ready to try out a more advanced filling system without breaking the bank.

The GO’s piston-filling mechanism can hold more ink than cartridges or converters, so you’ll be able to write for pages and pages. However, be sure to plan ahead (or keep an emergency vial of ink on you), because the last thing you want is to run out of ink in the middle of a test!

The Best Fountain Pen Inks for Note-Taking: Herbin Perle Noire Inks
Herbin Perle Noire Ink is an excellent all-purpose black ink, and it works great for note-taking, too.

Shop Now

Herbin Perle Noire is the JetPens team’s favorite all-purpose black ink, so it’s no wonder that we recommend it for note-taking, too. It performs well with fast dry times and very little feathering or bleedthrough, even on low-quality papers like class handouts. Surprisingly, it only smears slightly under highlighters.

We appreciate that Perle Noire comes in standard international cartridges as well as two bottle sizes. You can try out a 10 ml bottle of ink to find out if you want to continue filling your pen from one.

Also Consider: Kaweco Pearl Black Inks

Kaweco Pearl Black is another all-purpose pick from our Best Black Fountain Pen Inks guide. Just like Herbin Perle Noire, it dries quickly and is well behaved on poor-quality papers. It doesn’t smear much under highlighters, either. We rank it slightly lower than our top pick because it’s not available in a sample size, so you’ll have to commit to an entire 50 ml bottle, or use the cartridges (which get used up quickly and are more expensive in the long run).

Keep in mind that most highlighters will smear fountain pen inks, so it’s important to test your combination. Check out our test results below to see how our fountain pens and inks performed with our highlighter recommendations; you may experience more smearing with other highlighters.

CONSIDERATIONS
Ink Color
Dark ink will be easier to read when you’re studying later.
Your note-taking pen should use ink that’s dark and easy to read. Black ink is a tried-and-true pick, but feel free to use your favorite colors for your personal notes. If you’ll be turning them in, check with your teacher to make sure that the color you’ve picked is okay to use.

Don’t go overboard on the colors, though; you may regret sparkling pink notes when it’s time to study. Try using a basic color like black or off-black for the majority of your notes, then pick a few contrasting colors to emphasize important information or vocabulary terms.

Ink Flow
A smooth-flowing ink means that you don’t have to press down on the pen’s tip to get a dark line.
A smooth-flowing ink means that you don’t have to press down on the pen’s tip to get a dark line. This relieves pressure on your hand so you’re less likely to experience hand cramps. Pens that use fluid inks such as rollerball or fountain pens are the best in terms of ink flow, but our other recommendations in this guide have been tested for this characteristic, too.
Quick Drying
Nobody likes messy, smeared notes, so a quick-drying ink is a must.
Nobody likes messy, smeared notes, so a quick-drying ink is a must. Water-based pens usually need at least a few seconds to dry, while oil-based ballpoint pens dry almost instantly. A fast-drying ink is especially useful for left-handed writers who tend to drag the side of their palm over freshly-written notes.
Tip Size
The right tip size for you will depend on your writing style.
The right tip size differs from person to person. Writers with small handwriting may want to use fine tips like 0.38 mm or 0.5 mm, while those with large handwriting will likely prefer broader tips like 0.7 mm or 1.0 mm. You may also want to switch to a broader tip size for bold headers, or a finer tip size to pack notes onto a teacher-approved cheat sheet.

Our picks in this JetPens guide tend to be on the finer side to help with dry times, but almost all of our recommendations have broad tip sizes available so you can pick what’s right for your writing style.

You can think of ink flow, dry time, and tip size as being three points on a triangle. Changing one characteristic will affect the way that the ink looks on the page. For example, a finer tip size puts down less ink, which dries faster. Meanwhile, a wetter ink will take more time to dry and could make your writing look thicker.

Highlighter Resistance
If you do a lot of highlighting, look for pens or highlighters that are formulated to resist smearing.
Going over your notes with a highlighter might cause them to smear. Water-based highlighter inks typically react with water-based inks like those found in gel pens, rollerball pens, and fountain pens.

If you do a lot of highlighting, look for pens or highlighters that are formulated to resist smearing. Oil-based ballpoint pens are safe bets because they usually don’t smear when highlighted. Gel and pencil highlighters won’t smear most inks.

Grip and Weight
A comfortable pen that isn’t too heavy will be easier to hold during long writing sessions.
It might seem obvious, but a comfortable grip section is comfortable to hold for long writing sessions. If you experience hand cramps while taking notes, look for padded, wide grips that encourage your fingers to relax. If you’re not used to heavy pens, they’re more tiring to hold, too. Stick with lightweight plastic or aluminum pens.
TEST RESULTS

We created our writing samples using 0.5 mm tip sizes, or a tip size as close to 0.5 mm as possible. We used fine nibs for the fountain pen samples. The Platinum Preppy’s sample was created using a Platinum Black Ink cartridge (which is included with some Preppy Fountain Pens). We paired Herbin Perle Noire and Kaweco Pearl Black with a fine TWSBI GO.

We tested smudging by running a finger over the ink immediately after writing. We also tested both of our highlighter picks on the dry writing samples. Tests were done on Rhodia DotPad paper, which is smooth and non-absorbent. More absorbent papers may experience less smearing.
